title: How Rockets Reach Space
summary: The idea of action and reaction, why rockets have stages and what makes an orbit.

steps.title: Push back, move forward
sentences: A rocket moves by throwing hot gas out of its bottom very fast.
Newton's third law says that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
The gas goes down, so the rocket goes up.

steps.title: Why not just go up?
sentences: To stay in orbit around Earth, a spacecraft must travel sideways at about 7.8 kilometres every second.
It is still falling toward Earth, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it.
That endless falling around the planet is an orbit.

steps.title: Stages
sentences: Rockets carry fuel, and fuel is heavy.
So a rocket is built in stages, and each empty stage is dropped off to make the rest lighter.
India's launch vehicles from ISRO use stages in exactly this way.

steps.title: Escape
sentences: To go all the way to the Moon, a spacecraft needs even more speed so that it can escape Earth's pull.
The speed needed to leave Earth altogether is about 11.2 kilometres every second.
That is called the escape velocity.

facts: Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in free fall, not because there is no gravity.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023.

quiz.q: What makes a rocket move up?
quiz.why: A rocket works by action and reaction, gas goes down and the rocket goes up. It works even in empty space.
Dropping empty tanks removes weight, so the rest can speed up more easily.

quiz.q: An orbit is best described as...
options: Falling around Earth while moving sideways fast
quiz.why: The spacecraft keeps falling but moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground.

notes: Speeds are rounded. Chandrayaan-3 landing on 23 August 2023 is a fixed historical fact.
